title: Mendelian & Population Genetics
description: Mendel's laws, cross ratios and probability, testcrosses, dominance patterns, ABO, epistasis, sex linkage, pedigrees, linkage and map units, chi-square, human genetic disorders, Hardy–Weinberg math and genetic drift.

cards.title: Which of Mendel's laws says the two alleles for a character separate during gamete formation, so each gamete gets just one?
cards.body:
The law of segregation

Its physical basis is that homologous chromosomes, which carry the two alleles, separate in anaphase I of meiosis.

Example: a heterozygote ($Aa$) makes $A$ and $a$ gametes in a $1:1$ ratio.
cards.searchQuery: Mendel law of segregation alleles separate gametes

cards.title: In a $Pp \times Pp$ cross (purple dominant to white), what fraction of the purple-flowered offspring are heterozygous?
cards.body:
$\frac{2}{3}$

Genotypes come out $1\,PP : 2\,Pp : 1\,pp$, so the phenotypes are $3$ purple : $1$ white. Of the $3$ purple, $2$ are $Pp$.

Watch out: $\frac{1}{2}$ is the fraction of **all** offspring that are $Pp$, not of the purple ones.
cards.searchQuery: Pp x Pp purple offspring fraction heterozygous 2/3

cards.title: How can you find out whether a purple-flowered pea plant (dominant phenotype) is $PP$ or $Pp$?
cards.body:
Do a testcross: breed it with a homozygous recessive ($pp$, white) plant.

All purple offspring means the plant is $PP$. About half white ($1:1$) means it is $Pp$.

Why: the $pp$ parent can only pass on $p$, so each offspring's phenotype reveals which allele the unknown parent gave.
cards.searchQuery: testcross homozygous recessive determine unknown genotype

cards.title: What phenotypic ratio comes from an $AaBb \times AaBb$ cross with two unlinked genes, each showing complete dominance?
cards.body:
$9:3:3:1$

The classes are $9\,A\_B\_ : 3\,A\_bb : 3\,aaB\_ : 1\,aabb$. Each gene alone gives $3:1$, and multiplying probabilities (for example $\tfrac{3}{4} \times \tfrac{3}{4} = \tfrac{9}{16}$ for $A\_B\_$) gives sixteenths.

Key idea: this is the signature of **independent assortment**; linkage or epistasis changes it.
cards.searchQuery: dihybrid cross 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio independent assortment

cards.title: With three unlinked genes, what fraction of the offspring from $AaBbCc \times AaBbCc$ will be $aabbcc$?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{64}$

By the **product rule**, each gene independently gives $\frac{1}{4}$ homozygous recessive, so $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{64}$.

Watch out: use the sum rule (add) when an outcome can arise in more than one mutually exclusive way. For $Aa$ from $Aa \times Aa$: $\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: product rule trihybrid cross aabbcc 1/64 probability

cards.title: Red snapdragons crossed with white ones give all pink offspring. What inheritance pattern explains this?
cards.body:
Incomplete dominance

The heterozygote shows an **intermediate** phenotype. Crossing two pinks gives $1$ red : $2$ pink : $1$ white, so the phenotype ratio equals the genotype ratio.

Watch out: it isn't blending, because red and white reappear. Contrast codominance, where both alleles show fully (for example AB blood type).
cards.searchQuery: incomplete dominance snapdragon pink flowers 1:2:1

cards.title: A type A parent and a type B parent have a type O child. What are the parents' genotypes?
cards.body:
$I^A i$ and $I^B i$ (both heterozygous); the child is $ii$.

Their children could be AB, A, B or O, each with probability $\frac{1}{4}$.

Key idea: ABO has three alleles. $I^A$ and $I^B$ are **codominant** (type AB shows both A and B carbohydrates), and both are dominant to $i$.
cards.searchQuery: ABO blood type inheritance type A and type B parents type O child

cards.title: Labradors with genotype $ee$ are yellow no matter which $B/b$ alleles they carry. What is this kind of gene interaction called?
cards.body:
Epistasis

The $E$ gene (whether pigment is deposited in fur) masks the $B$ gene (black vs. brown pigment).

Example: $BbEe \times BbEe$ gives $9$ black : $3$ brown : $4$ yellow instead of $9:3:3:1$.
cards.searchQuery: epistasis Labrador coat color 9:3:4 ratio

cards.title: A woman who carries an X-linked recessive allele has children with an unaffected man. What fraction of their sons will be affected?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

Each son gets one of his mother's two X chromosomes (and his father's Y). No daughters are affected, but half are carriers.

Why: males need only one copy because they're **hemizygous**, so disorders like hemophilia and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are far more common in males.
cards.searchQuery: X-linked recessive carrier mother sons affected 1/2

cards.title: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. What mode of inheritance must the trait have?
cards.body:
Autosomal recessive, with both parents carriers (heterozygous)

It can't be dominant: an affected child would need an affected parent. It can't be X-linked recessive: an affected daughter would need an affected father.

Tip: unaffected parents with an affected child always point to a **recessive** trait.
cards.searchQuery: pedigree unaffected parents affected daughter autosomal recessive

cards.title: Mendel's law of independent assortment holds for genes on different chromosomes. What kind of genes tend to break it?
cards.body:
Linked genes

These are genes close together on the same chromosome, which tend to be inherited together. Only crossing over separates them, producing recombinant offspring.

Key idea: genes far apart on one chromosome recombine so often (up to $50\%$) that they assort as if unlinked.
acceptedAnswers: genes close together on the same chromosome
cards.searchQuery: linked genes same chromosome independent assortment exception

cards.title: A testcross yields $2{,}000$ offspring, $160$ of them recombinant for two genes. How far apart are the genes on a linkage map, in map units? (number only)
cards.body:
$8$ map units (centimorgans)

Recombination frequency $= \dfrac{160}{2000} = 8\%$, and $1\%$ recombination equals $1$ map unit ($1\,\mathrm{cM}$).

Watch out: frequencies top out at $50\%$, and map units measure crossover frequency, not physical distance.
cards.searchQuery: map units centimorgans recombination frequency calculation testcross

cards.title: Write the two Hardy–Weinberg equations and say what each term stands for.
cards.body:
$p + q = 1$ gives allele frequencies; $p^2 + 2pq + q^2 = 1$ gives genotype frequencies.

- $p$: frequency of the dominant allele; $q$: frequency of the recessive allele.
- $p^2$: homozygous dominant; $2pq$: heterozygous; $q^2$: homozygous recessive.

Key idea: if the population is in equilibrium, genotype frequencies follow directly from allele frequencies.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg equations p + q = 1 p squared 2pq q squared

cards.title: List the five conditions a population must meet to stay in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium.
cards.body:
No mutation, random mating, no natural selection, a very large population and no gene flow.

1. No mutations.
2. Random mating.
3. No natural selection.
4. Extremely large population (no genetic drift).
5. No gene flow.

Why: if any one is violated, allele or genotype frequencies can change from generation to generation.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium five conditions assumptions

cards.title: A recessive disorder affects $1$ in $10{,}000$ newborns. Assuming Hardy–Weinberg, about what percentage of people are carriers? (nearest whole percent, number only)
cards.body:
$2\%$ (about $1$ in $50$)

Since $q^2 = 0.0001$, $q = 0.01$ and $p = 0.99$. Carriers are $2pq = 2 \times 0.99 \times 0.01 \approx 0.0198$.

Watch out: using $q^2$ or $q$ as the carrier frequency, or forgetting to take the square root first.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg carrier frequency 1 in 10000 recessive disorder 2pq

cards.title: A few individuals colonize an island, and by chance a rare mainland allele becomes common there. Which kind of genetic drift is this?
cards.body:
The founder effect

The small founding group's allele frequencies differ from the source population's by chance.

Key idea: the **bottleneck effect** is a related kind of drift, in which a disaster or habitat loss drastically shrinks a population, as with Illinois's greater prairie chickens. Drift is strongest in small populations.
cards.searchQuery: founder effect genetic drift small colonizing population

cards.title: What are the alternative versions of a gene, found at the same locus, called?
cards.body:
Alleles

A diploid organism has two alleles of each gene, one inherited from each parent.

Example: the gene for flower color in peas has a purple allele and a white allele.
cards.searchQuery: allele definition alternative versions of a gene

cards.title: What term describes an organism's observable traits, as opposed to its genetic makeup?
cards.body:
Phenotype

The genetic makeup is the **genotype**. Phenotype results from genotype plus environment.

Example: $PP$ and $Pp$ pea plants have different genotypes but the same phenotype (purple).
cards.searchQuery: phenotype versus genotype definition

cards.title: An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is called what?
cards.body:
Homozygous

Examples are $PP$ and $pp$. A $Pp$ organism is **heterozygous**.

Key idea: a homozygote makes only one kind of gamete for that gene; a heterozygote makes two kinds.
cards.searchQuery: homozygous heterozygous definition alleles

cards.title: What do we call an allele whose phenotype appears in a heterozygote, masking the other allele?
cards.body:
A dominant allele

The masked allele is **recessive**, and it shows only when homozygous.

Watch out: dominant does not mean common or "stronger". Many harmful dominant alleles, such as the one for Huntington's disease, are rare.
cards.searchQuery: dominant allele definition masks recessive allele heterozygote

cards.title: What term describes plants that produce offspring identical to themselves for a trait when self-pollinated?
cards.body:
True-breeding

These lines are homozygous for the trait, so Mendel used them as the **P generation** to start his crosses.

Key idea: crossing two different true-breeding lines gives the $F_1$ generation, and crossing $F_1$ plants with each other gives the $F_2$.
cards.searchQuery: true-breeding Mendel P generation homozygous pea plants

cards.title: Mendel crossed true-breeding purple-flowered and white-flowered peas and let the $F_1$ self-pollinate. What was the $F_2$ phenotypic ratio of purple to white?
cards.body:
$3:1$

The $F_1$ plants were all $Pp$ and all purple, because purple is dominant. Self-pollinating them gave $\frac{3}{4}$ purple and $\frac{1}{4}$ white.

Key idea: the white trait vanished in $F_1$ and reappeared in $F_2$, so the factors for it must stay intact in heterozygotes.
cards.searchQuery: Mendel F2 generation 3:1 ratio purple white peas

cards.title: Give three reasons garden peas were a good choice for Mendel's experiments.
cards.body:
They have easily distinguished traits, are easy to cross-pollinate or self-pollinate, and have a short generation time.

- Traits come in clear either/or forms (purple or white).
- He could control pollination.
- Each cross produced many offspring, so ratios were meaningful.

Key idea: large numbers of offspring matter because ratios such as $3:1$ are only approximate in small samples.
cards.searchQuery: why Mendel used pea plants advantages

cards.title: What is the specific physical location of a gene on a chromosome called?
cards.body:
A locus

Homologous chromosomes carry alleles of the same genes at the same loci.

Key idea: the plural is **loci**.
cards.searchQuery: locus gene location chromosome definition

cards.title: A heterozygote ($Aa$) is crossed with a homozygous recessive ($aa$). What fraction of the offspring are $aa$?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

The $Aa$ parent makes $A$ and $a$ gametes equally, and the $aa$ parent gives only $a$. So the offspring are $\frac{1}{2}\,Aa$ and $\frac{1}{2}\,aa$.

Key idea: this is a **testcross**, so the phenotypic ratio is $1:1$.
cards.searchQuery: Aa x aa cross offspring ratio 1:1 testcross

cards.title: Two heterozygotes ($Aa$) mate. What fraction of their offspring are homozygous recessive?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{4}$

Each parent gives $a$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, so $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

Watch out: $\frac{1}{4}$ is the chance for each child. A family of four children need not contain exactly one affected child.
cards.searchQuery: Aa x Aa monohybrid cross probability aa offspring one quarter

cards.title: What is the genotypic ratio $AA : Aa : aa$ from an $Aa \times Aa$ cross?
cards.body:
$1:2:1$

The Punnett square has four equally likely boxes: $AA$, $Aa$, $aA$ and $aa$. The two heterozygous boxes combine.

Key idea: with complete dominance, the phenotypic ratio ($3:1$) collapses the genotypes $AA$ and $Aa$ together.
cards.searchQuery: genotypic ratio 1:2:1 monohybrid cross Aa x Aa Punnett square

cards.title: A cross between a dominant-phenotype plant and a recessive-phenotype plant gives offspring in a $1:1$ ratio. What are the parents' genotypes?
cards.body:
$Aa \times aa$

A recessive-phenotype parent must be $aa$. To get recessive offspring, the other parent must carry an $a$, so it is $Aa$.

Tip: any $1:1$ ratio from a single gene points to a heterozygote crossed with a homozygous recessive.
cards.searchQuery: infer parent genotypes 1:1 offspring ratio Aa x aa

cards.title: Two parents with the dominant phenotype produce offspring in a $3:1$ dominant : recessive ratio. What are their genotypes?
cards.body:
$Aa \times Aa$

Recessive offspring show that both parents carry an $a$. Both are dominant in phenotype, so both are heterozygous.

Tip: a $3:1$ ratio from a single gene means both parents are heterozygous.
cards.searchQuery: 3:1 ratio parents genotypes both heterozygous Aa x Aa

cards.title: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive allele plan three children. What is the probability that at least one child is affected?
cards.body:
$\frac{37}{64}$

Each child is affected with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, so unaffected with $\frac{3}{4}$. All three unaffected: $\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)^3 = \frac{27}{64}$.

Tip: use the **complement**: $1 - \frac{27}{64} = \frac{37}{64} \approx 0.58$.
cards.searchQuery: probability at least one child affected two carriers recessive three children

cards.title: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive allele have three children. What is the probability that exactly two are affected?
cards.body:
$\frac{9}{64}$

One particular arrangement (say, first two affected, third unaffected) has probability $\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 \times \frac{3}{4} = \frac{3}{64}$.

There are $3$ such arrangements, which are mutually exclusive, so add them: $3 \times \frac{3}{64} = \frac{9}{64}$.
cards.searchQuery: binomial probability exactly two of three children affected carriers recessive

cards.title: A couple has had three sons. What is the probability that their fourth child is a son? (fraction)
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

Each birth is an independent event, so earlier children don't change the probability.

Watch out: this is the gambler's fallacy. The chance of four sons in a row is $\frac{1}{16}$ **before** any are born, but once three have been born, the next is still $\frac{1}{2}$.
cards.searchQuery: independent events probability fourth child son gambler's fallacy genetics

cards.title: In an $Aa \times Aa$ cross, what is the probability that an offspring is homozygous (either $AA$ or $aa$)?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

The two outcomes are mutually exclusive, so use the **sum rule**: $P(AA) + P(aa) = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2}$.

Key idea: use the product rule for "and" with independent events, and the sum rule for "or" with exclusive events.
cards.searchQuery: sum rule probability homozygous offspring Aa x Aa

cards.title: What term is used for the phenotype that is most common in natural populations?
cards.body:
The wild type

Variants that differ from it are called **mutants**.

Watch out: wild-type alleles are not always dominant. Some wild-type alleles are recessive to a mutant allele.
cards.searchQuery: wild type phenotype most common in natural populations

cards.title: A heterozygous tall pea plant ($Tt$, tall dominant) self-pollinates and produces $160$ offspring. About how many do you expect to be short? (number only)
cards.body:
$40$

Short plants are $tt$, with probability $\frac{1}{4}$, so $\frac{1}{4} \times 160 = 40$.

Watch out: this is only an expected value. Real counts vary around it by chance, which is why statistical tests like chi-square are used.
cards.searchQuery: expected offspring count Tt self cross tall short 160 plants

cards.title: A testcross of a purple-flowered plant (purple dominant) gives $52$ purple and $48$ white offspring. Is the unknown parent homozygous dominant or heterozygous?
cards.body:
Heterozygous ($Pp$)

A testcross with $pp$ gives about $1:1$ if the unknown is heterozygous, and all purple if homozygous dominant. White offspring show the plant carries $p$.

Key idea: even one white offspring proves heterozygosity, whereas many purple offspring can only suggest $PP$.
cards.searchQuery: testcross results 1:1 purple white unknown genotype Pp

cards.title: An individual is heterozygous for $n$ independently assorting genes. How many genetically different gametes can it make? (formula in $n$)
cards.body:
$2^n$

Each heterozygous gene sends one of two alleles into a gamete, and independent genes multiply: $2 \times 2 \times \cdots = 2^n$.

Example: $AaBbCc$ gives $2^3 = 8$ gamete types.

Watch out: homozygous genes add no variety, so only count the heterozygous ones.
cards.searchQuery: number of gamete types 2^n heterozygous genes independent assortment

cards.title: An individual is heterozygous at $5$ independently assorting genes and homozygous at $2$ others. How many different gamete types can it produce? (number only)
cards.body:
$32$

Only the heterozygous genes count: $2^5 = 32$.

Tip: the homozygous genes contribute a factor of $1$ each.
cards.searchQuery: gamete types heterozygous five genes homozygous two genes count

cards.title: A dihybrid is testcrossed with a double homozygous recessive, and the two genes assort independently. What is the expected offspring ratio of the four phenotypes?
cards.body:
$1:1:1:1$

The dihybrid makes four gamete types ($AB$, $Ab$, $aB$, $ab$) in equal numbers, and the recessive parent adds only $ab$. So each offspring class is equally likely.

Key idea: if the testcross shows something other than $1:1:1:1$, the genes are probably **linked**.
cards.searchQuery: dihybrid testcross 1:1:1:1 ratio independent assortment

cards.title: From a cross of two $AaBb$ parents (unlinked genes), what fraction of offspring show the dominant phenotype for the first gene and the recessive phenotype for the second?
cards.body:
$\frac{3}{16}$

The dominant phenotype for the first gene has probability $\frac{3}{4}$, and the recessive for the second $\frac{1}{4}$. Multiply: $\frac{3}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{3}{16}$.

Tip: solve gene by gene and multiply, rather than drawing a $16$-box square.
cards.searchQuery: dihybrid cross fraction A_bb 3/16 forked line method

cards.title: From a cross of two $AaBb$ parents (unlinked genes), what fraction of offspring are heterozygous for both genes?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{4}$

Each gene gives heterozygotes with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, so $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{4}$.

Watch out: this is a **genotype** question. Among the four phenotypes, the $\frac{9}{16}$ with both dominant traits include $AABB$, $AaBB$, $AABb$ and $AaBb$.
cards.searchQuery: dihybrid cross fraction offspring double heterozygous AaBb 1/4

cards.title: In an $RrYy \times RrYy$ pea cross ($R$ round, $Y$ yellow, both dominant), about how many of $160$ offspring seeds are expected to be wrinkled and green? (number only)
cards.body:
$10$

Wrinkled green is $rryy$, with probability $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{16}$. So $\frac{160}{16} = 10$.

Key idea: this is the $1$ in the $9:3:3:1$ ratio.
cards.searchQuery: expected number wrinkled green seeds dihybrid cross 9:3:3:1 160

cards.title: Which of Mendel's laws states that alleles of different genes are distributed into gametes independently of one another?
cards.body:
The law of independent assortment

It applies to genes on different chromosomes, or far enough apart on the same chromosome. It rests on the random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I.

Watch out: it does not hold for linked genes.
cards.searchQuery: Mendel law of independent assortment different genes gametes

cards.title: Two unlinked genes are crossed as $AaBb \times Aabb$. What fraction of the offspring are $aabb$?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{8}$

Take each gene separately. $Aa \times Aa$ gives $aa$ with probability $\frac{1}{4}$. $Bb \times bb$ gives $bb$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$.

Multiply: $\frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{8}$.
cards.searchQuery: AaBb x Aabb cross fraction aabb offspring product rule

cards.title: How many different genotypes can result from a cross of two $AaBb$ parents with unlinked genes? (number only)
cards.body:
$9$

Each gene gives $3$ genotypes ($AA$, $Aa$, $aa$), so $3 \times 3 = 9$.

Key idea: there are $9$ genotypes but only $4$ phenotypes with complete dominance.
cards.searchQuery: number of genotypes dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb nine genotypes

cards.title: What pattern of inheritance describes a heterozygote in which both alleles are fully and separately expressed?
cards.body:
Codominance

Both phenotypes show up distinctly, not blended.

Example: a person with genotype $I^A I^B$ makes both A and B carbohydrates on red blood cells (type AB), and a roan cow has both red and white hairs.
cards.searchQuery: codominance definition both alleles expressed ABO blood group

cards.title: How many different genotypes are possible for the ABO blood group gene (alleles $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$)? (number only)
cards.body:
$6$

The genotypes are $I^AI^A$, $I^Ai$, $I^BI^B$, $I^Bi$, $I^AI^B$ and $ii$.

Key idea: there are only $4$ phenotypes (A, B, AB, O), because $I^AI^A$ and $I^Ai$ both give type A, and $I^BI^B$ and $I^Bi$ both give type B.
cards.searchQuery: ABO blood group six genotypes four phenotypes alleles

cards.title: A person with type AB blood and a person with type O blood have children. Which blood types are possible, and in what proportions?
cards.body:
Half type A and half type B; no children are AB or O.

The AB parent ($I^AI^B$) gives $I^A$ or $I^B$ equally, and the O parent ($ii$) gives only $i$.

So the children are $I^Ai$ (type A) or $I^Bi$ (type B), each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$.

Watch out: this is a common exam question showing that an AB parent can never have an O child.
cards.searchQuery: AB x O blood type cross children possible blood types

cards.title: What term describes a single gene that affects several seemingly unrelated phenotypic traits?
cards.body:
Pleiotropy

A mutation in one gene can disrupt a protein used in many tissues.

Example: sickle-cell disease causes anemia, pain crises and organ damage from a single allele. Marfan syndrome, from a connective-tissue gene, affects the skeleton, eyes and aorta.
cards.searchQuery: pleiotropy one gene multiple traits sickle cell Marfan

cards.title: What term describes a trait, such as human height or skin color, that is influenced by many genes and varies continuously?
cards.body:
Polygenic inheritance

The alleles of many genes each add a small effect, so phenotypes form a smooth range, often a bell-shaped curve.

Watch out: environment also contributes, so polygenic traits are also called **quantitative** or multifactorial traits.
cards.searchQuery: polygenic inheritance continuous variation height skin color

cards.title: What term describes the percentage of individuals with a particular genotype who show the expected phenotype?
cards.body:
Penetrance

If only $80\%$ of people with a dominant allele show the trait, penetrance is $80\%$ (incomplete penetrance).

Watch out: penetrance is all-or-none for each person, while **expressivity** is how strongly a trait shows in those who have it.
cards.searchQuery: penetrance definition percentage with genotype showing phenotype expressivity

cards.title: What term describes the degree to which a phenotype is shown among individuals who all carry the same genotype?
cards.body:
Expressivity

It can vary widely, from mild to severe, even within a single family.

Example: polydactyly can appear as an extra finger on one hand only, or on both hands and feet.
cards.searchQuery: variable expressivity definition genotype phenotype severity

cards.title: Hydrangeas with identical genotypes bloom blue in acidic soil and pink in basic soil. What is the range of phenotypes a single genotype produces across environments called?
cards.body:
The norm of reaction

A genotype does not fix a phenotype, only a range of possible ones.

Key idea: phenotype depends on **genotype and environment** together, so multifactorial traits are only partly heritable.
cards.searchQuery: norm of reaction hydrangea environment phenotype range genotype

cards.title: In mice, the $A^Y$ allele gives yellow fur and is dominant, but $A^YA^Y$ embryos die. Crossing two yellow mice gives what ratio of surviving yellow : agouti offspring?
cards.body:
$2:1$

The cross is $A^YA \times A^YA$ (agouti is $AA$). The expected genotypes are $\frac{1}{4}\,A^YA^Y$, $\frac{1}{2}\,A^YA$ and $\frac{1}{4}\,AA$.

The $A^YA^Y$ class dies, leaving $2$ yellow ($A^YA$) to $1$ agouti ($AA$).

Key idea: a ratio of $2:1$ in place of $3:1$ is the signature of a recessive lethal allele.
cards.searchQuery: lethal allele yellow mice 2:1 ratio agouti Ay

cards.title: In sweet peas, purple flowers need a dominant allele at both of two genes; otherwise the flowers are white. What phenotypic ratio of purple : white comes from $AaBb \times AaBb$?
cards.body:
$9:7$

Purple requires $A\_B\_$, which is $\frac{9}{16}$ of the offspring. Everything else ($3 + 3 + 1 = 7$) is white.

Key idea: this is **complementary gene action**, a form of epistasis in which the two genes must both be functional.
cards.searchQuery: sweet pea epistasis 9:7 ratio complementary genes purple white

cards.title: In summer squash, dominant $W$ gives white fruit and masks color; $ww$ plants are yellow ($Y\_$) or green ($yy$). What white : yellow : green ratio comes from $WwYy \times WwYy$?
cards.body:
$12:3:1$

$W\_$ is $\frac{12}{16}$ and is white regardless of $Y$. Of the $ww$ plants ($\frac{4}{16}$), $\frac{3}{16}$ are $wwY\_$ (yellow) and $\frac{1}{16}$ are $wwyy$ (green).

Key idea: here a **dominant** allele is epistatic, unlike the recessive epistasis ($9:3:4$) in Labradors.
cards.searchQuery: dominant epistasis summer squash 12:3:1 ratio

cards.title: How does epistasis differ from dominance?
cards.body:
Dominance is an interaction between alleles of the same gene; epistasis is an interaction between different genes.

In epistasis, the alleles at one gene mask or modify the effect of alleles at another gene.

Watch out: epistasis changes dihybrid ratios, such as $9:3:4$, $9:7$ or $12:3:1$, even though the genes still assort independently.
cards.searchQuery: epistasis versus dominance difference genes alleles

cards.title: Which gene on the human Y chromosome triggers the development of male characteristics?
cards.body:
$SRY$ (sex-determining region Y)

Its product switches on the genes that turn the embryonic gonads into testes.

Key idea: in humans, sex depends on whether $SRY$ is present, not on the number of X chromosomes.
cards.searchQuery: SRY gene Y chromosome male development sex determination

cards.title: What term describes the state of a male's X-linked genes, which are present in only one copy?
cards.body:
Hemizygous

A male has one X and one Y, so a single recessive X-linked allele is enough to show the trait.

Watch out: the words homozygous and heterozygous do not apply to a male's X-linked genes.
cards.searchQuery: hemizygous males X-linked genes one copy

cards.title: An affected father (X-linked recessive trait) and a homozygous unaffected mother have children. What fraction of their daughters are carriers?
cards.body:
All of them

Every daughter gets the father's X, which carries the recessive allele, and a normal X from the mother.

Key idea: none of the sons is affected, because they get the father's Y and the mother's normal X.
cards.searchQuery: X-linked recessive affected father daughters all carriers sons unaffected

cards.title: A carrier mother and an affected father (X-linked recessive trait) have children. What fraction of their daughters are affected?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{2}$

The mother gives a normal or a mutant X with equal probability, and the father always gives his mutant X to daughters.

So half the daughters are carriers and half are affected. Half the sons are also affected.
cards.searchQuery: X-linked recessive carrier mother affected father daughters affected 1/2

cards.title: Can an X-linked allele be passed directly from a father to his son? (yes or no)
cards.body:
No

A father gives his Y chromosome to his sons, and his X to his daughters.

Tip: in a pedigree, father-to-son transmission rules out X-linked inheritance.
cards.searchQuery: X-linked inheritance father to son transmission not possible

cards.title: What is the condensed, inactive X chromosome in the cells of a female mammal called?
cards.body:
A Barr body

Early in development one X in each cell is randomly inactivated. All descendants of that cell keep the same X silenced.

Example: calico cats are mosaics, with some patches expressing one coat-color allele and other patches the other.
cards.searchQuery: Barr body X inactivation female mammals calico cats

cards.title: Which scientist's work with white-eyed fruit flies provided the first evidence that a specific gene is carried on a specific chromosome (the X)?
cards.body:
Thomas Hunt Morgan

He found that the white-eye trait was inherited with sex: it appeared mostly in males.

Key idea: this linked a trait to a chromosome and supported the chromosome theory of inheritance.
cards.searchQuery: Thomas Hunt Morgan white eyed Drosophila X-linked first evidence

cards.title: A trait is carried on the Y chromosome. Which offspring of an affected father show it?
cards.body:
All of his sons, and none of his daughters

The Y passes only from father to son, so the trait appears only in males, in every generation.

Key idea: Y-linked genes are rare, because the human Y carries relatively few genes.
cards.searchQuery: Y-linked inheritance father to all sons pattern

cards.title: In a pedigree, every affected person has an affected parent and the trait appears in every generation, in both sexes equally. What is the likely mode of inheritance?
cards.body:
Autosomal dominant

The trait does not skip generations, and unaffected parents never have affected children.

Tip: affected parents can have unaffected children if they are heterozygous ($Aa \times aa$).
cards.searchQuery: pedigree autosomal dominant every generation affected parent

cards.title: A trait is far more common in males, skips generations, and passes from an affected father to his grandsons through his unaffected daughters. What is the likely mode of inheritance?
cards.body:
X-linked recessive

Fathers never pass the trait directly to sons. Their daughters become carriers and can pass it on to their own sons.

Tip: look for mostly affected males, no father-to-son transmission and carrier daughters.
cards.searchQuery: pedigree X-linked recessive pattern affected males skip generations

cards.title: Mitochondrial DNA is passed to children by which parent?
cards.body:
The mother

The egg supplies almost all of the cytoplasm and its mitochondria, while the sperm contributes essentially none.

Key idea: in a pedigree, an affected mother passes the trait to all of her children, and an affected father to none.
cards.searchQuery: mitochondrial DNA inherited from mother maternal inheritance pedigree

cards.title: A man and a woman are each unaffected, but each has a sibling with an autosomal recessive disease (their parents are unaffected). What is the probability that their first child is affected?
cards.body:
$\frac{1}{9}$

Each unaffected person is a carrier with probability $\frac{2}{3}$. The child is affected only if both are carriers and both pass on the allele: $\frac{2}{3} \times \frac{2}{3} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{9}$.

Watch out: use $\frac{2}{3}$, not $\frac{1}{2}$. Because each person is unaffected, $aa$ is ruled out, so the remaining genotypes are $AA$ (1 part) and $Aa$ (2 parts).
cards.searchQuery: probability child affected both parents siblings affected autosomal recessive 2/3 carrier

cards.title: Why does marriage between close relatives raise the risk of autosomal recessive disorders in children?
cards.body:
Relatives share a recent ancestor, so they are more likely to carry the same rare recessive allele.

Their child is therefore more likely to inherit two copies of it, one through each parent.

Example: first cousins share about $\frac{1}{8}$ of their alleles, so the risk of a recessive disorder is noticeably higher than for unrelated parents.
cards.searchQuery: consanguinity first cousins increased risk recessive disorders shared alleles

cards.title: What term describes offspring whose combination of alleles differs from both parents' because of crossing over?
cards.body:
Recombinants

Offspring with the parental combinations are called **parental types**.

Key idea: for linked genes, recombinants are always the minority classes in a testcross.
cards.searchQuery: recombinant offspring crossing over parental types linked genes

cards.title: What is the maximum recombination frequency between two genes, no matter how far apart they are on a chromosome? (percent)
cards.body:
$50\%$

At $50\%$ the genes assort independently, just like genes on different chromosomes.

Watch out: map distances can add up to more than $50$ map units for far-apart genes, but the observed recombination frequency never exceeds $50\%$.
cards.searchQuery: maximum recombination frequency 50 percent independent assortment linkage

cards.title: Three linked genes have map distances $A$–$B$ = $10$, $B$–$C$ = $6$ and $A$–$C$ = $16$ map units. Which gene lies in the middle? (letter)
cards.body:
$B$

In a linear map, the two shorter distances add up to the longest one: $10 + 6 = 16$. The two genes at the ends, $A$ and $C$, are farthest apart.

So the order is $A$–$B$–$C$.

Tip: find the largest distance; the gene not in that pair is in the middle.
cards.searchQuery: genetic map gene order three genes map units additive middle gene

cards.title: A dihybrid testcross gives $420$ and $410$ offspring of the two parental types, and $85$ of each recombinant type. What is the distance between the genes in map units? (number only)
cards.body:
$17$

Recombinants $= 85 + 85 = 170$, out of $420 + 410 + 170 = 1000$ offspring.

Recombination frequency $= \frac{170}{1000} = 17\%$, so the genes are $17$ map units apart.

Tip: identify the two largest classes as parental, and the two smallest as recombinant.
cards.searchQuery: calculate recombination frequency testcross offspring counts map units problem

cards.title: In a testcross involving two linked genes, which offspring classes are the most numerous: parental types or recombinant types?
cards.body:
Parental types

The parental combinations are inherited together unless a crossover happens between the genes, so the recombinant classes are always the smaller pair.

Key idea: if all four classes are about equal ($1:1:1:1$), the genes are unlinked.
cards.searchQuery: testcross linked genes parental classes most numerous recombinant fewest

cards.title: Write the chi-square statistic used to test whether observed offspring counts fit an expected ratio.
cards.body:
$\chi^2 = \sum \dfrac{(O - E)^2}{E}$

Here $O$ is the observed count and $E$ is the expected count for each class.

Watch out: use counts, not percentages or ratios. Compare the result with a critical value for the right degrees of freedom.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test formula genetics observed expected counts

cards.title: A cross is expected to give a $3:1$ ratio. Of $100$ offspring, $80$ show the dominant trait and $20$ the recessive trait. What is $\chi^2$ (to two decimal places)?
cards.body:
$1.33$

Expected counts: $75$ and $25$. Then $\chi^2 = \dfrac{(80-75)^2}{75} + \dfrac{(20-25)^2}{25} = 0.33 + 1.00 = 1.33$.

With $1$ degree of freedom, the critical value at $p = 0.05$ is $3.84$. Since $1.33 < 3.84$, the data fit a $3:1$ ratio, and you fail to reject the hypothesis.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square test 3:1 ratio calculation 80 20 offspring

cards.title: How many degrees of freedom does a chi-square test have when testing a $9:3:3:1$ dihybrid ratio? (number only)
cards.body:
$3$

Degrees of freedom equal the number of phenotype classes minus one: $4 - 1 = 3$.

Key idea: the critical value at $p = 0.05$ for $3$ degrees of freedom is $7.81$.
cards.searchQuery: chi-square degrees of freedom classes minus one 9:3:3:1 critical value 7.81

cards.title: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, $16\%$ of individuals show a recessive phenotype. What is the frequency $q$ of the recessive allele? (decimal)
cards.body:
$0.4$

The recessive phenotype is $q^2 = 0.16$, so $q = \sqrt{0.16} = 0.4$.

Tip: start from the recessive phenotype, the only class you can count directly, then take a square root.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg find q from recessive phenotype frequency square root

cards.title: In the same kind of population, $16\%$ show a recessive phenotype ($q^2 = 0.16$). What fraction of the population is heterozygous? (decimal)
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg heterozygote frequency 2pq worked example q squared 0.16

cards.title: A dominant allele has frequency $p = 0.7$ in a Hardy–Weinberg population. What fraction of individuals are homozygous dominant? (decimal)
cards.body:
$0.49$

The homozygous dominant frequency is $p^2 = 0.7^2 = 0.49$.

Watch out: $p^2$ is not the fraction showing the dominant phenotype. That is $p^2 + 2pq = 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91$.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg p squared homozygous dominant frequency p equals 0.7

cards.title: A population of $100$ has $40$ $AA$, $40$ $Aa$ and $20$ $aa$ individuals. What is the frequency of allele $A$? (decimal)
cards.body:
$0.6$

Count alleles: there are $200$ in total. $A$ appears $2 \times 40 + 40 = 120$ times, so $\frac{120}{200} = 0.6$.

Tip: each homozygote has two copies and each heterozygote has one.
cards.searchQuery: calculate allele frequency from genotype counts population genetics

cards.title: For that population ($40$ $AA$, $40$ $Aa$, $20$ $aa$; $p = 0.6$, $q = 0.4$), do the genotype frequencies fit Hardy–Weinberg expectations? (yes or no)
cards.body:
No

Hardy–Weinberg predicts $p^2 = 0.36$ $AA$, $2pq = 0.48$ $Aa$ and $q^2 = 0.16$ $aa$. The observed $0.40$, $0.40$ and $0.20$ are different.

Key idea: the population has fewer heterozygotes than expected, a sign of nonrandom mating such as inbreeding.
cards.searchQuery: test Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium observed vs expected genotype frequencies

cards.title: About $1$ in $12$ males has red–green color blindness (X-linked recessive). Assuming Hardy–Weinberg, about what percentage of females are affected? (nearest tenth of a percent, number only)
cards.body:
$0.7\%$

For males, the affected frequency equals the allele frequency, so $q = \frac{1}{12} \approx 0.083$. Females need two copies, so $q^2 \approx 0.0069 \approx 0.7\%$.

Key idea: X-linked recessive disorders are far more common in males: $q$ vs. $q^2$.
cards.searchQuery: X-linked recessive Hardy-Weinberg color blindness males females frequency q squared

cards.title: What is the maximum possible frequency of heterozygotes ($2pq$) for a gene with two alleles in a Hardy–Weinberg population? (decimal)
cards.body:
$0.5$

$2pq$ is largest when $p = q = 0.5$, giving $2 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.5$.

Watch out: rare alleles are found mostly in heterozygotes: when $q$ is small, $2pq \approx 2q$ is far larger than $q^2$.
cards.searchQuery: maximum heterozygote frequency 2pq 0.5 when p equals q Hardy-Weinberg

cards.title: An autosomal gene has unusual genotype frequencies, then a large population mates randomly with no other forces acting. After how many generations are genotypes in Hardy–Weinberg proportions?
cards.body:
$1$

One generation of random mating produces the proportions $p^2$, $2pq$ and $q^2$, and they stay there.

Key idea: allele frequencies are unchanged by random mating. Only the genotype proportions adjust.
cards.searchQuery: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium reached in one generation of random mating

cards.title: Cystic fibrosis affects about $1$ in $2{,}500$ people of European ancestry and is autosomal recessive. What is the recessive allele frequency $q$, assuming Hardy–Weinberg? (decimal)
cards.body:
$0.02$

$q^2 = \frac{1}{2500} = 0.0004$, so $q = \sqrt{0.0004} = 0.02$.

Example: carriers are then $2pq \approx 2 \times 0.98 \times 0.02 \approx 0.039$, about $1$ in $25$ people.
cards.searchQuery: cystic fibrosis 1 in 2500 allele frequency Hardy-Weinberg carriers 1 in 25

cards.title: In a Hardy–Weinberg population with $q = 0.1$, what percentage of all copies of the recessive allele are carried by heterozygotes? (number only)
cards.body:
$90\%$

In $100$ people, $q^2 = 1$ is $aa$ ($2$ copies) and $2pq = 18$ are $Aa$ ($18$ copies). So $\frac{18}{20} = 90\%$.

Key idea: selection against a rare recessive trait removes alleles slowly, because most copies are hidden in carriers.
cards.searchQuery: rare recessive alleles hidden in heterozygotes carriers percent Hardy-Weinberg

cards.title: How does inbreeding affect allele frequencies and genotype frequencies in a population?
cards.body:
It leaves allele frequencies unchanged but increases homozygotes and reduces heterozygotes.

Mating among relatives makes offspring more likely to inherit two copies of the same allele from a common ancestor.

Watch out: inbreeding alone is not evolution, but increased homozygosity exposes harmful recessive alleles (inbreeding depression).
cards.searchQuery: inbreeding effect on genotype frequencies increases homozygosity allele frequencies unchanged

cards.title: What term describes random changes in allele frequencies from one generation to the next, especially in small populations?
cards.body:
Genetic drift

By chance alone, some alleles are passed to more offspring than expected from their frequency.

Key idea: drift is random, so unlike natural selection it does not tend to improve adaptation.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift definition random allele frequency change small populations

cards.title: What term describes the loss of genetic variation after a sudden event drastically shrinks a population?
cards.body:
The bottleneck effect

The survivors are a random sample, so their allele frequencies may differ from the original population's, and rare alleles may be lost entirely.

Example: northern elephant seals, hunted to fewer than $100$ individuals in the 1890s, now have very low genetic variation.
cards.searchQuery: bottleneck effect genetic drift reduced genetic variation elephant seals

cards.title: Is genetic drift stronger in small populations or in large populations?
cards.body:
Small populations

With fewer individuals, chance events cause larger swings in allele frequency, just as a few coin flips stray further from $50\%$ heads than many flips do.

Key idea: this is why Hardy–Weinberg requires a very large population.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift stronger in small populations law of large numbers

cards.title: If genetic drift is the only force acting, what is the long-term fate of an allele in a finite population?
cards.body:
It will eventually be lost or fixed (reach a frequency of $1$).

Over time, drift reduces genetic variation within a population and increases differences between isolated populations.

Example: the lower an allele's starting frequency, the more likely it is to be lost rather than fixed.
cards.searchQuery: genetic drift allele fixation or loss long-term effect finite population

cards.title: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in a gene for which chloride channel protein? (abbreviation)
cards.body:
CFTR

The gene is on chromosome $7$, and the disease is autosomal recessive. Faulty chloride transport leaves thick mucus in the lungs and pancreas.

Example: the most common allele, $\Delta F508$, deletes one phenylalanine.
cards.searchQuery: cystic fibrosis CFTR chloride channel chromosome 7 autosomal recessive

cards.title: Tay-Sachs disease, an autosomal recessive disorder, results from a deficiency of which lysosomal enzyme?
cards.body:
Hexosaminidase A

Without it, a lipid called GM2 ganglioside builds up in nerve cells and damages the brain.

Watch out: carriers have about half the normal enzyme activity but are healthy, which illustrates why recessive disorders skip generations.
cards.searchQuery: Tay-Sachs hexosaminidase A deficiency lysosomal GM2 ganglioside

cards.title: Huntington's disease is autosomal dominant and fatal, so why does the allele persist in the population?
cards.body:
Symptoms usually begin after age $30$–$50$, often after people have had children.

So carriers usually pass the allele on before selection can act against it.

Key idea: a child of an affected heterozygous parent has a $\frac{1}{2}$ chance of inheriting the allele.
cards.searchQuery: Huntington disease autosomal dominant late onset persists in population

cards.title: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a deficiency of which enzyme?
cards.body:
Phenylalanine hydroxylase

Without it, phenylalanine builds up and can cause intellectual disability. A low-phenylalanine diet started in infancy prevents the damage.

Example: newborn screening finds PKU early, so affected children can be treated.
cards.searchQuery: phenylketonuria PKU phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency autosomal recessive

cards.title: Hemophilia A, an X-linked recessive disorder, is caused by a deficiency of which clotting factor?
cards.body:
Factor VIII

Affected males bleed excessively because their blood clots slowly.

Watch out: hemophilia B involves factor IX instead.
cards.searchQuery: hemophilia A factor VIII deficiency X-linked recessive

cards.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy, an X-linked recessive disorder, results from absence of which muscle protein?
cards.body:
Dystrophin

The $DMD$ gene is very large, so new mutations are common. Without dystrophin, muscle fibers are easily damaged.

Key idea: because it is X-linked recessive, it mainly affects boys.
cards.searchQuery: Duchenne muscular dystrophy dystrophin X-linked recessive DMD gene

cards.title: Pattern baldness is caused by an autosomal allele that is expressed differently in males and females. What kind of trait is this?
cards.body:
A sex-influenced trait

The gene is on an autosome, but sex hormones change whether the allele acts as dominant or recessive.

Watch out: do not confuse it with a **sex-linked** trait, whose gene lies on a sex chromosome.
cards.searchQuery: sex-influenced trait pattern baldness autosomal versus sex-linked
